# Handoff: take OrcaSlicer 2.5.0 into JusPrin

Written 2026-11-07. This is a temporary working doc: keep it untracked, don't commit it.

## The goal

JusPrin is built on OrcaSlicer 2.4.2. Upstream released 2.5.0 as its official stable release on 2026-11-07.
Kenneth wants JusPrin on 2.5.0 before JusPrin's first release, so we don't launch on a version upstream has
already replaced. The job is done when the fork's main branch contains 2.5.0, builds on Mac, Windows and
Linux, and passes the checks listed under "Verification" below.

## Where things stand

- The fork follows upstream's release branches, not `upstream/main`. Today it contains `upstream/release/v2.4`
  up to v2.4.2 (commit 8500fcdcca). 2.5.0 is the tip of `upstream/release/v2.5.0` (tag v2.5.0, commit 40ecc66f78).
- `jusprin-newui` is the fork's main branch. `ui-walkthrough` carries newer work on top of it (10 commits when this was written). Ask Kenneth which
  one the merge should go into, and whether other work should land first.
- JusPrin changes 58 upstream-owned files (about 865 lines added, 74 removed). Everything else it adds lives in
  new files, mostly under `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/`.

## Proposed approach, and why

Kenneth agreed to this: **one merge commit that takes v2.5.0, using v2.4.2 as the merge base.** The procedure is now
rule 10 in `agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md` (commit "Fork stewardship: take upstream releases by merging
from the last release taken"). Here is the reasoning, so you can judge it yourself:

- **A plain `git merge v2.5.0` is wrong for this fork.** The 2.4 and 2.5 release branches each split off upstream's
  development line on their own, so git picks a June 2026 development commit (3ffb9585d2) as the base. That merge
  conflicts in about 3,900 files: roughly 3,800 vendor profiles plus translations and CI files. None of them are ours.
- **Naming v2.4.2 as the base limits the merge to what JusPrin changed.** That gives 22 conflicted files with about
  38 conflict spots. `Plater.cpp` has 9 of them; most other files have 1 to 3.
- **Replaying our commits gets the same 22 files but costs more.** The doc used to say to replay. A linear replay of
  the 417 JusPrin commits could stop up to 59 times, because that many commits touch a conflicted file. Many of
  those stops would land on lines we rewrote later ourselves: 22 commits touch `Plater.cpp`, adding 556 lines and
  deleting 328, while the net change is only 252 added and 22 deleted. A squash replay avoids the repeat stops,
  but both kinds of replay rewrite history, and every branch in the roughly 20 worktrees would need rebasing.
- **The merge rewrites nothing.** I built a trial merge commit without resolving its conflicts and merged
  `ui-walkthrough` into it: zero conflicts. Afterwards a plain `git merge` of a later 2.5.x patch release
  computes v2.5.0 as its base, so a 2.5.1 needs no special handling.

I also checked that git's normal tools can do this. In a throwaway worktree, writing v2.5.0's commit into
`MERGE_HEAD` and running `git merge-recursive v2.4.2 -- HEAD v2.5.0` stopped at the same 22 files and showed a
normal merge in progress (git 2.50.1). I didn't resolve or commit anything there.

**Push back if you find a reason.** Two examples: a resolution comes out wrong because `merge-recursive` misses a
rename that a normal `git merge` would catch, or something in the history makes the base override give a
misleading result. Tell Kenneth what you found and what you would do instead. He has agreed to the merge
approach, but only on the evidence above.

## Things I noticed that you'll need to judge

- **Conflicts that aren't line edits.** Upstream deleted `build_release_vs.bat` and builds Windows through
  `build_win.bat` now. Our version added error checks (`if errorlevel 1 goto :failed`), so decide whether those
  checks belong in the new script. Upstream also added a `.agents` folder where the fork has a `.agents` file.
  `AGENTS.md` conflicts as well.
- **Dependencies.** 2.5.0 adds six dependencies (python3 for plugins, Assimp, FFMPEG, SLVS, DataChannel and
  wxInspector) and changes OpenSSL, OCCT, TBB, PNG and wxWidgets. The existing `deps/build` probably won't link,
  so plan for a dependency rebuild on each platform. It's likely the slowest part. Follow "Building on a shared
  machine" in `AGENTS.md`: other sessions build on the same Mac.
- **New upstream features that might touch JusPrin's shell.**
  - Python plugins can add whole panels and menus.
  - The Design tab is a new experimental CAD tab, off by default.
  - The Design tab has an MCP control socket, enabled only by the environment variable `ORCA_CAD_MCP`, so an
    outside AI agent can drive it. That's separate from JusPrin's own MCP server.

  JusPrin hides OrcaSlicer's tab strip and wraps `MainFrame`, so check what these features look like inside
  JusPrin's shell.
- **The resolution rule.** For each conflict, say whether the obvious resolution is correct or loses something.
  That's the stewardship doc's "Before you finish" step. JusPrin-specific seams in `Plater.cpp`, `GUI_App` and
  `MainFrame` are where a wrong resolution would break behavior silently.

## Verification

The stewardship doc lists what has to pass after every upstream update:
- the full native build on all three platforms
- the focused contract tests
- the real multi-plate workflow
- native gizmo input
- the stock-behavior regression checks

The AGENTS.md test commands also apply. For changes to text the model reads, the live suite applies too. One test
already fails on `jusprin-newui`: a crash in the placeholder `coFloatsOrPercents` test, inherited from upstream.
Note whether 2.5.0 fixes it.

Kenneth's rules that apply: reproduce before fixing, don't commit submodule updates, and don't push without being
asked. Ask him how and where to land the result.

A JusPrin git worktree builds against the already-built deps by configuring:

```
cmake -B build/arm64 -G "Ninja Multi-Config" -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=arm64 -DCMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=15.0 \
  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local;/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local" \
  -DSLIC3R_GUI=ON -DSLIC3R_STATIC=ON -DSLIC3R_PCH=ON -DBUILD_TESTS=ON \
  -DCMAKE_AR=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ar -DCMAKE_RANLIB=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ranlib
```

CMAKE BINARY (2026-09-29): configure with `/Applications/CMake.app/Contents/bin/cmake` (put it first on PATH). Homebrew's cmake 4.1 at /opt/homebrew/bin fails with "Could NOT find Eigen3 (missing: EIGEN3_VERSION_OK) (Required is at least version 5.0.1)", and a failed configure poisons the cache: `rm -rf build` before retrying.

The two `CMAKE_AR`/`CMAKE_RANLIB` flags are required on a FRESH build dir:
without them Apple's ar is used and liblibslic3r_gui.a (>4 GiB in
RelWithDebInfo) fails to archive. They only work at first configure, not on
reconfigure. Full story: agent-docs/macos-build-troubleshooting.md. See
[[liblibslic3r-gui-4gib-ar-limit]].

FRESH WORKTREE TRAP (2026-09-18): building only `shell_integration_harness`
does not build the web pages. Also build `--target jusprin_web jusprin_catalogs`
(needs node on PATH: /Users/kenneth/.nvm/versions/node/v24.13.0/bin). Without
them resources/jusprin/{home,agent}/index.html are missing, no web views are
created, and the harness silently tests something else (printer panel starts
shown; web-view crashes vanish).

`BUILD_TESTS=ON` is required or the tests/ tree (workspace, shell targets) is
not generated. Build with `cmake --build build/arm64 --config RelWithDebInfo
--target <targets>`. wxWidgets 3.3 sources for API verification live under
/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/dep_wxWidgets-prefix/.

CWD TRAP (cost real time once): the harness resets the Bash cwd to the main
repo /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin between turns, so a *relative*
`cmake --build build/arm64` silently builds the MAIN repo's build dir, not the
worktree's — the worktree binary then runs stale code and a re-fix looks like it
"didn't take". Always pass the worktree build dir as an ABSOLUTE path to
`cmake --build /…/.claude/worktrees/<wt>/build/arm64 …`, and run test binaries by
absolute path. Also: `cmake --build --target <one_exe>` may relink against a
stale lib without recompiling a changed .cpp in that lib — build the app target
(e.g. OrcaSlicer) too so the lib recompiles; verify with
`grep -c '<file>.cpp.o' build.log`. Editing tools (Edit/Write) use absolute
paths so source edits land correctly regardless of cwd.

STALE PROMPT TRAP (2026-09-23): `--target shell_integration_harness` does NOT
rebuild the web pages, so a harness run after an edit to AgentUI (for example
printerInstructions.ts) loads the old bundle. Six --printer-live runs were
wasted this way. After any page edit, build `jusprin_web` explicitly and check
the new text is in resources/jusprin/agent/index.html before running live.

DISK (2026-10-10): building with `--config Release` instead of RelWithDebInfo made a fresh worktree build dir 859 MB instead of ~14 GB, needed no llvm-ar relink, and the shell harness ran normally from `tests/shell/Release/`. Use it when the disk is nearly full (it was at 99%) and no debugger is needed. With other sessions building, a fresh build took far longer than usual (machine load 30 to 85).

    - MainFrame's positional TabPosition indices are gone; tabs have names

      MonitorPanel::ensure(), since that selection also updates the sidebar.

      menus find it by its label there. Without this the shell declined to

An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.

Facts specific to OrcaSlicer, worth knowing before choosing where to put a seam. They change over time; re-measure rather than trusting these.

File-level churn is only a first approximation: some functions inside `Plater.cpp` have not been touched upstream in the entire life of this fork, and a seam there is far cheaper than the file's overall rate suggests. Some native state is shared rather than owned by one object. ### Contract tests

Test strong IDs, invalid/missing/stale identifiers, command errors, subscription lifetime, event coalescing, revision behavior, and fake-workspace history without linking the GUI. Test both successful and unsuccessful commands, and assert that reported results agree with authoritative state.

### Real-adapter application tests

A fake cannot validate `Plater`, `GLCanvas3D`, plate membership, `GUI_ObjectList` dependencies, event ordering, or Orca's undo stack. Add an application-level harness that loads deterministic project fixtures and covers:

- project-ready signaling rather than fixed event-loop delays;
- a dedicated application name and bundle identity so UI automation cannot target another Orca build;
- an isolated temporary configuration and repository-owned fixture;
- deterministic on-bed object placement, active tab, selection, and camera-visible state before reporting readiness;
- object and viewport selection in both directions;
- rename, duplicate, remove, plate switch, import, undo, and redo;
- committed native transform and exact-value transform;
- callback snapshots at the advertised revision;
- subscriber destruction;
- project replacement and session-ID invalidation;
- operations initiated outside the adapter.

The POC self-test is evidence and test-design input, not a production harness: its STL setup could not reproduce rename undo, and it intentionally terminated through `std::_Exit`.

### Shell end-to-end tests

Run the complete native application with a deterministic multi-plate project. Verify the visible real canvas, camera controls, selection, native gizmos, Slice, Check print, return to Prepare, undo/redo, object pane synchronization, Agent pane persistence, resize, maximize/restore, and the unchanged legacy layout when testing a compatibility mode.

Visual appearance alone is insufficient. Validate state from authoritative callbacks and pair visibility claims with screenshots or rendered evidence.

Use the harness to establish deterministic application state; use UI automation
for real pointer, keyboard, focus, and rendering checks rather than for fragile
startup setup. For canvas policy, inventory every overlay surface and verify
rendering and hit-testing separately. Compare a stock window with the product
policy, then exercise selection, orbit, pan, zoom, active gizmo input, slicing,
Preview, and restoration of the prior presentation state.

### Printer tests without hardware

Bambu paths (printer-menu Idle / Printing / Offline, Select Machine, print job)
are exercised by an in-process fake that substitutes for the Bambu printer
agent while a real Bambu Lab **system** preset stays selected. How to turn it
on, the JSON control file, isolated-instance rules for agents, and acceptance
checks: [Fake Bambu README](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md).

Print-host paths (Moonraker and OctoPrint) run against the real host software
in Docker, with simulated printer boards:
[print hosts README](../../tests/printer_hosts/README.md). Do not add a fake
Bambu network layer (MQTT/FTPS/discovery) without an explicit request.

# Test suite rules

Rules for writing tests under `tests/`. [CATCH2.md](CATCH2.md) is the Catch2 reference. Building and running the suites is covered on the wiki, at <https://www.orcaslicer.com/wiki/developer_reference/how_to_test.html>.

## The suites

- `libslic3r`: the core library. Geometry, meshes, file formats, config and presets, Clipper, algorithms, data structures.
- `fff_print`: the FFF slicing pipeline, from a `Model` plus config through `Print` and `PrintObject` to emitted G-code.
- `sla_print`: SLA support-tree and pad geometry, support-point generation, raycast.
- `libnest2d`: 2D nesting and packing.
- `slic3rutils`: the Python plugin system and its slicing-pipeline bindings.
- `filament_group`: filament-to-extruder grouping, checked against golden files.
- `cli`: end-to-end runs of the built `orca-slicer` binary, Linux only. These tests carry the `RequiresApp` label, which the CI unit-test job excludes because it receives only `build/tests`; run them with `ctest --test-dir build/tests -C Release -L RequiresApp`.

## Building and running

Tests are off by default, so the build has to be told to include them.

- Windows: `build_win.bat -ds --run-tests`, which builds the dependencies and the tests and runs them (`-l -x` for the clang-cl and Ninja build CI uses)
- macOS: `./build_release_macos.sh -s -a arm64 -T`, which builds and runs them
- Linux: `./build_linux.sh -t`, then `ctest --test-dir build/tests -C Release`

Rebuild a single suite with `cmake --build build --config Release --target <suite>_tests`. Visual Studio, Xcode and the Ninja Multi-Config generator that `build_linux.sh` uses are all multi-configuration, so `ctest` needs `-C` on every platform; without it, tests registered with plain `add_test()` lose their labels and report "Not Run".

## Where a test goes

- Pick the suite by the production code the test exercises, not by how the test is written.
- A property of a class that holds with no `Print` involved belongs in `libslic3r`. Behavior that depends on print settings, or produces or consumes G-code or slicing state, belongs in `fff_print`.
- One file per subsystem, named `test_<subsystem>.cpp`. It owns every test for that subsystem, whether the test reads in-memory state or generated output.
- When you add a file, list it in that suite's `CMakeLists.txt` in the same change.

## Use the existing helpers

Check these before writing your own setup or output-parsing code.

- `tests/test_utils.hpp` is shared by every suite. `load_model()` loads a mesh from `tests/data/`, and `ScopedTemporaryFile` gives a temp path that removes itself.
- `fff_print/test_helpers.hpp` builds and slices a `Print` and parses the emitted G-code. Read it before writing an fff_print test rather than assembling a `Print` by hand.
- The other suites have their own: `sla_print/sla_test_utils.hpp`, `libnest2d/libnest2d_test_utils.hpp`, `slic3rutils/plugin_test_utils.hpp`, `filament_group/fg_test_utils.hpp`. `libslic3r` has none and uses the shared header.
- Test data lives in `tests/data/` and is reached through the `TEST_DATA_DIR` define. Wrap it in `std::string(...)` before joining a path onto it.

## Writing the test

- Name the test case as a plain behavioral sentence in the present tense. No `Subsystem:` prefix.
- Tag it with the subsystem it covers, matching the file, in PascalCase. That tag is what people filter on, so every test needs one.
- Add further tags where they help: a narrower one to slice a large file (`[Rotcalip]`, `[Placer]`), a shared one for something spanning files (`[Python]`, `[H2C]`, `[Regression]`), or `[NotWorking]` / `[.]` to disable or hide a test. Say why in a comment if you disable or hide.
- Prefer a flat `TEST_CASE` per behavior, with `GENERATE` for parameterized cases. Reserve `SCENARIO` / `GIVEN` / `WHEN` / `THEN` for genuine shared setup that branches into a few close variations.
- Set the config keys your test depends on, and derive the expected values from what you set. A 20mm cube sliced at `layer_height` 2 is 10 layers, and the test should state both parts. If a number in your assertion comes from a key you never set, the test is also testing that default.
- Assert the defining property, not an incidental value. "Skirt present" or "at least 2 brim loops" survives a refactor; exact coordinates and byte counts do not.
- Name a regression test for the behavior it protects, never for an issue or PR number.
- When asserting on G-code, match the meaningful token such as `; skirt` rather than whole lines, whitespace or comment wording. Depend on ordering only when ordering is the contract.

## Catch2 rules that cause real breakage

- Never reuse a `SECTION` name inside a loop. Use `DYNAMIC_SECTION` so each iteration is unique.
- Never assert from a spawned thread. Catch2 assertions are not thread-safe. Collect results in the thread and assert on the main thread.
- Never combine conditions with `&&` or `||` inside one assertion. Split them so Catch2 can print both operands on failure.
- Compare floats with `WithinAbs` or `WithinRel`, never `==`. Prefer these over `Approx` in new tests.
- Keep tests self-contained: no shared state, green under `--order rand`.

A `cmake --build` started with the Bash tool's `run_in_background` is still
bound by that call's `timeout` (default 120 s, max 600 s). When it fires the
build log ends with `ninja: build stopped: interrupted by user.` and `exit=130`,
which looks like a human Ctrl-C but is the harness. Seen 2026-09-14 on a
725-step JusPrin rebuild.

**Why:** the notification says "completed" and the log shows no compiler
error, so it is easy to misread as a finished build; the changed files had not
compiled at all.

**How to apply:** for anything longer than a few minutes, start it detached
(`nohup sh -c "cmake --build … > log 2>&1; echo exit=\$? >> log" & disown`),
then arm a Monitor on the log that reports progress and the `exit=` line. Check
`grep -c '<file>.cpp.o' log` before trusting the result. Related:
[[track-wall-clock-on-background-work]], [[jusprin-worktree-build]].

    set(CMAKE_XCODE_ATTRIBUTE_GCC_WARN_64_TO_32_BIT_CONVERSION "NO")

    # The Xcode generator ignores CMAKE_<LANG>_COMPILER_LAUNCHER, so hand the launcher to
    # Xcode's own Compiler Launcher setting, which wraps every clang compile (C, C++,
    # Objective-C++ and the precompiled header) with one program: the C++ launcher wins when
    # both are set. The setting takes a single program path, not a CMake launcher list.
    # Xcode versions without it ignore it and build uncached.
    if (CMAKE_GENERATOR STREQUAL "Xcode")
        if (CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER)
            set(CMAKE_XCODE_ATTRIBUTE_C_COMPILER_LAUNCHER "${CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER}")
        elseif (CMAKE_C_COMPILER_LAUNCHER)
            set(CMAKE_XCODE_ATTRIBUTE_C_COMPILER_LAUNCHER "${CMAKE_C_COMPILER_LAUNCHER}")

    endif ()
    if (CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_ID MATCHES "Clang" OR CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_VERSION VERSION_GREATER 6.0)
        list(APPEND warnings_disabled ignored-attributes)       # from Eigen headers marked SYSTEM
    endif ()
    if (CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_ID STREQUAL "GNU")

    foreach (w IN LISTS warnings_disabled)

content.text:
I found the cause of the second failure. OrcaSlicer 2.5.0's new Design tab takes the address of the accent colour, `&ImGuiWrapper::COL_ORCA`. The fork changed `COL_ORCA` on 2026-10-21, from a constant into a function call that returns a fresh copy, so the brand accent can be set at runtime. clang refuses to take the address of that copy. Microsoft's compiler allows it, which is why the Windows build passed.

The fix I plan stays in the fork's own lines in `ImGuiWrapper.hpp`: `col_orca()` will return a reference to a stored colour that's refreshed on each read, the same way the other accent shades next to it already work. That leaves upstream's Design tab code untouched. I'll apply it once the keep-going build has listed every failure.

content.text:
I've pulled `claude/upstream-2.5.0` into its own worktree and built it on this Mac. Most of the tests have run, and the last few checks are still going.

**Building.** Building took fixes in two places.
- **Mac setup, no code change:** this Mac had no dependencies built for OrcaSlicer 2.5.0, so I built them in the worktree. One of them, GMP, only built once I set `SDKROOT` to the macOS SDK path.
- **The merge branch:** the app wouldn't compile at first. OrcaSlicer 2.5.0 now turns compiler warnings into errors with clang and gcc, but not with Microsoft's compiler. That's why the merge session's Windows build passed and this one didn't. I fixed six kinds of failure, all in fork-owned files or fork-added lines:
  - Fork build files included `deps_src` as a normal include path, so warnings from the bundled JSON header broke the build. I now include it as a system header, the way OrcaSlicer includes its bundled libraries.
  - JusPrin changed `COL_ORCA` into a function call that returns a fresh copy of the accent colour. 2.5.0's new Design tab takes the address of `COL_ORCA`, which clang refuses for a temporary copy. It now returns a stored copy, and the upstream Design tab code is untouched.
  - Smaller fixes: two lambdas captured structured bindings (a C++20 feature), and there was an unused field and several unused lambda captures. The unused captures are spread over `OrcaHomeBackend.cpp`, `PrinterMenu`, `FakeWorkspace.hpp`, `OrcaPrinterBackend.cpp` and the shell harness.
  - One real bug: in the shell harness, `press_tool_strip` kept a reference into a temporary list that was destroyed before the next line used it. That bug is on `jusprin-newui` too.
- After these fixes, the app and every test target build. The fixes are uncommitted in the worktree.

**Tests so far:**
- **Native tests:** 3,813 of 3,820 passed. All seven failures were in upstream tests, during a stretch when the machine's load average hit 184. Most of that load came from other sessions and a virtual machine. Run one at a time, six of the seven pass in 1 to 4 seconds each. The last one, "Surface centering survives changes to separated infill settings", is rerunning now.
- **Placeholder test:** the `coFloatsOrPercents` test that crashes on `jusprin-newui` now passes, so 2.5.0 fixes it.
- **Web pages:** all tests pass, 687 for the Agent page and 155 for Home.
- **MCP Python tests:** the one repeatable failure is a Linux packaging test whose expected tool list doesn't include `print_dialog_open`. It also fails on `jusprin-newui`: `tests/mcp` is identical on both branches, and that tool was added there without updating the test. So the merge didn't cause it.
- **Shell harness default run:** in progress. 430 checks have passed and none have failed so far. It's on the second slice.

**Still to do:** finish the shell harness run, run the workspace harness and the MCP bridge check, and then launch the real app to check the multi-plate workflow and gizmo input.

Every build of the fork (and /Applications/OrcaSlicer.app) shares bundle id `com.softfever3d.orca-slicer`. The desktop-control tools resolve an app by bundle id and bind to whichever instance comes first, so `app_list_windows` returns `[]` and filtered screenshots hide the window you actually launched.

**Working recipe (2026-09-05):** `ditto` the built .app into the scratchpad, `plutil -replace CFBundleIdentifier -string com.jusprin.worktree-test`, `codesign --force --deep -s -`, then `open -n <copy>.app --args <model>` and `request_access` for the new id. `app_screenshot`/`app_click` then work and include popup menus. A display-scope `left_click` on the header did NOT open the fork's PopupWindow menus, but a background `app_click` did; take the pixel-level `zoom` with the display tools afterwards (call `app_release` first). Display-scope `Escape` does not close those popups; a click elsewhere does.

The MCP discovery file `~/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2/jusprin/mcp.json` points at the newest instance's `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp`; `tests/mcp/probe.py`'s `call()` can drive real tools (e.g. `workspace_inspect`, then `report_slice_review` with sessionId/plateId/sliceResultId) to put the header into the Check-print state without lldb. lldb `expr` cannot call inline accessors like `status_row()`.

app." Both messages are about Spaces, so the natural read is that the user is sitting in
a full-screen app — but with *Displays have separate Spaces* on, a window merely sitting
on the second monitor produces exactly the same symptoms. Kenneth was not in full screen;
the harness had opened on the Acer.

Tell them apart before saying anything to the user: take a **display-scope** screenshot
(`app_release`, then `computer_batch` screenshot). Its header names the monitor it

content.text:
The `claude/upstream-2.5.0` branch builds and runs on this Mac, but only after fixes the merge needed and didn't have. Most are compile fixes. One fixes a visible problem: OrcaSlicer's own toolbar was showing inside the JusPrin screen. All 13 fixes are uncommitted in the worktree.

**Why the Mac build failed.** OrcaSlicer 2.5.0 treats compiler warnings as errors on clang and gcc. The merge was only checked on Windows, where the compiler isn't held to that rule, so about 56 errors went unnoticed. I fixed them in fork code and tests. Most were unused lambda captures and missing `SYSTEM` markers on include folders. Two fixes matter more:
- `ImGuiWrapper.hpp`: the fork's `COL_ORCA` macro produced a temporary value, and 2.5.0's new `DesignCanvas.cpp` takes its address. It now returns a stored copy, so the upstream file stays untouched.
- `shell_harness.cpp`: a test kept a reference to a temporary object after it was destroyed. That bug is on newui too.

**The toolbar problem.** When I opened a model in the real app, OrcaSlicer's main toolbar and gizmo toolbar were drawn over the JusPrin 3D view. The newui build doesn't do this. The cause: 2.5.0 moved those toolbars into a new drawing function, `_render_overlay_toolbars()`, which the fork's hide-the-old-overlays switch didn't cover. I added one guard in `GLCanvas3D.cpp` so that switch skips the new function too. Before adding it, I compared the two versions to confirm nothing else had moved into that function. After the fix the toolbars are gone. Selecting the cube and clicking Move in JusPrin's tool strip opens the position panel and the gizmo arrows. Typing X = 20 moved the cube and added "Set Position" to the chat.

**Test results**
- C++ tests: 3813 of 3820 passed. The other 7 pass when run alone. Six of them were slow tests that timed out while the machine was heavily loaded. The seventh, the SSL certificate path test, needs network access and upstream marks it as not working.
- A slicer test that used to crash, the placeholder test for percent-or-float option lists, now passes. So 2.5.0 fixes that crash.
- Web page tests: 687 of 687 for the AI chat page and 155 of 155 for Home.
- Shell harness, which drives the real app through a two-plate project, slicing, the tool strip and undo: all 620 checks pass after the toolbar fix.
- Bridge harness, which tests the connection between the app and the AI tools: passes.
- Workspace harness: 11 checks fail, and the newui build fails the same 11 on this Mac, so the merge didn't cause them. Two are about dropping a second model into a project; those also fail on Windows. The other nine are calibration checks: on this Mac, generating a flow, pressure-advance or temperature calibration gives the project a new identity instead of keeping the old one. Windows passed these, so they're specific to this Mac and predate the merge.
- `tests/mcp`'s Linux package test expects the list of AI tools without `print_dialog_open`, a tool newui added. That's out of date on newui too.

**Still open.** These are proposals, not done work:
- Look into the Mac-only calibration identity failures.
- Add `print_dialog_open` to the expected tool list in the Linux package test.
- Note in the stewardship doc that checking a merge on Windows alone misses clang's warnings-as-errors.

I didn't look into why the splash screen shows version 2.5.0.
Yes, commit

result.output:
Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.
### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge
**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.
**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.
### 10. Take each upstream release by merging from the release we last took
**Rule.** Take a new upstream release with a merge whose base is the upstream release the fork last took. Never run a plain `git merge` of upstream, and never rewrite the fork's history to take a release.
**Mechanism.** The fork follows upstream's release branches, and each release branch splits off upstream's development line on its own. A plain merge picks the common ancestor itself, a development-line commit from before both release branches. Its conflict list is then everything that differs between the two release branches: vendor profiles, translations, CI files, none of it ours. Naming the last release we took as the base limits the merge to the fork's own changes. That gives the same conflicts a replay would hit, resolved once, with no commits rewritten, so branches in progress merge forward without a rebase. Measured on 2026-11-07, going from v2.4.2 to v2.5.0: 22 conflicted files either way, and a branch in progress merged into the trial result with no conflicts.
git merge-recursive <last release taken> -- HEAD <new release>
Resolve the conflicts, then `git commit`. A later patch release on the same release branch, such as 2.5.1 after 2.5.0, needs no override: a plain `git merge` finds the right base.
**The test.** Is the merge base the release we last took, and not a commit on upstream's development line?
**Violation.** `git merge upstream/main` or `git merge v2.5.0` with no base given. Each produces thousands of conflicts in files JusPrin never edited.
   git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<last release taken> <newest upstream release> HEAD
An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.

content.text:
I'd keep all of them as they are. Folding them into the merge commit is ruled out, and folding them into each other loses more than it gains.

**Squashing into the merge commit (`a75b67bcb4`).** The merge commit is already pushed to `origin/claude/upstream-2.5.0`. Folding fixes into it means rewriting it and force-pushing. Rule 10 of the fork stewardship doc says "never rewrite the fork's history to take a release". The reason: branches in progress merge forward from that merge commit, and a rewrite would force each of them to rebase. The merge also stays easier to review as only the conflict resolutions.

**Squashing the follow-up commits together.** The branch already has 11 fix commits after the merge, one per problem: building against the 2.5.0 APIs, settings questions, Speed Dial, and so on. They're all pushed, so squashing them also needs a force-push. My two new commits follow the same pattern and aren't pushed, so merging those two would cost nothing. I'd still keep them apart:
- The toolbar commit is the only one of the two that changes an OrcaSlicer-owned line. On its own, a future rebase can find it with `git log` on `GLCanvas3D.cpp` and read why the guard exists. Mixed into 12 files of compiler fixes, that note gets buried.
- If the guard ever needs reverting, for example because upstream moves the toolbars again, it can be reverted without touching the build fixes.

**Landing on main is a separate question.** How the whole branch lands on `main`, whether by a no-fast-forward merge or a squash, is still yours to decide. My memory notes say the old landing rule was removed and you want to be asked each time. Nothing about these commits needs settling now.
